persona.who: 21, Indian-American senior at Rutgers, born in NJ. Parents from Gujarat. Dating a white classmate; hasn't told parents. Feels neither fully Indian nor American.
persona.note: my parents keep asking when I'll 'settle down with a nice Gujarati boy' and I've been with my boyfriend for 2 years and he's not Indian. I feel like whichever way I go I lose a part of me

understanding.bridge: The smaller self they keep asking you to become is what the Gita warns against: a life lived to please others, not to know your own truth.
understanding.week_thesis: Seven days from being asked to shrink to standing in the truth of who you are, with the words to say so.

week_beats.hook: You recognise being asked to choose and the ache of it, named without blame.

understanding.core_struggle: A young woman is being asked to choose between her parents' expectation of a Gujarati boy and the two-year relationship she has built, and feels she loses a part of herself either way.
understanding.mirror: Whichever way you go, a part of you is left behind, and the question is which part they are asking you to leave.
understanding.insight: The love you have built is real, and the question your parents keep asking is not about your happiness but about their comfort with a story they did not write.
understanding.mechanism_label: Being seen as less than you are

queries.hook: My parents' expectations weigh on me. Being seen as less than you are by the people who ought to know you best, and the anger of watching the life you built get called a phase.
queries.diagnose: When others see only a role they have written for you, their picture is their smallness, not your measure; the harm deepens only when their picture starts to replace your own.
queries.steady: What you are cannot be cut smaller by what they see; your worth was never theirs to grant, and standing in your own truth is itself the duty.
queries.act: Speak the true thing gently and firmly, hold your ground on what is yours, and do your own duty without shrinking to fit the picture they hold.
queries.story: A woman who loved outside the boundaries her family drew, who stood in her truth and found her footing, and whose love was proven real.

verse.speaker: Sita
verse.setting: Abandoned because of gossip, Sita sends a message back to Ram.
verse.sanskrit: अहं तु नानुशोचामि स्वशरीरं नरर्षभ॥ यथापवादः पौराणां तथैव रघुनन्दन।
verse.line: It isn't the hardship I mind most. It's what people are saying that wasn't true.
verse.translation: I do not grieve for myself, best of men, so much as for the slander the people are spreading.
verse.why: Injustice from those we love is real grief; a stranger's kindness can become home.
verse.misuse: Sita is the one wronged here; the verse names unjust gossip, not her fault.

prasang.title: Sita left in the forest
prasang.summary: Hearing that people gossip about Sita's time in Lanka, Ram orders Lakshman to leave her, pregnant, near Valmiki's hermitage. Lakshman obeys in anguish. Sita grieves that she is cut off from everyone and slandered though innocent. Valmiki finds her, says he knows she is blameless, and tells her to treat his home as her own.
prasang.story_hook: Lakshman stopped the chariot at the river and could not bring himself to say why.
prasang.lesson: Injustice from those we love is real grief; a stranger's kindness can become home.

verse.meaning: Sita, in the forest, sends a message to Ram through Lakshman. She is alone, pregnant, and cut off from everyone. She tells him she does not grieve for her own hardship. What hurts her is the false gossip people are spreading about her time away. The verse says that injustice from those we love is real grief. A stranger’s kindness can become home.
verse.for_you: Your parents are asking you to choose, but the gossip is not about you. It is about their comfort. A stranger’s kindness can become home. Let that be your footing today.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on acting free of ego, like and dislike, in your own way.
verse.sanskrit: श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात् । स्वधर्मे निधनं श्रेयः परधर्मो भयावहः ॥
verse.line: Better your own path done imperfectly than someone else's done perfectly. Borrowed lives are dangerous.
verse.translation: Better is one's own duty, even done imperfectly, than the duty of another well done. Better is death in one's own duty; the duty of another is full of fear.
verse.why: Your own path, imperfectly walked, beats a borrowed one.
verse.misuse: Not 'stay in the role your family or birth assigned you'. It's about being true to your own nature and calling.

prasang.title: The ignorant and the wise; act free of like and dislike
prasang.summary: Krishna contrasts the attached and the wise, warns that ego claims credit for what nature does, and says to follow your own path rather than imitate another's.
prasang.lesson: Your own path, imperfectly walked, beats a borrowed one.

verse.meaning: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna, who is frozen on the battlefield, wondering if he should take up the life of a warrior or become a monk. Krishna says that a life lived to copy another is full of fear, while your own path, even if it is imperfect, is better. Borrowing someone else's life is dangerous because you will always be afraid of being found out.
verse.for_you: You are being asked to become someone else's story, and that borrowed life is already making you afraid. Your own path, with its real doubts and real love, is the only one that will ever fit you.

verse.speaker: Vidula
verse.setting: Queen Vidula rouses her son, who lies defeated and despairing after losing his kingdom.
verse.sanskrit: माऽऽत्मानमवमन्यस्व मैनमल्पेन बीभरः / मनः कृत्वा सुकल्याणं मा भैस्त्वं प्रतिसंहर
verse.line: Don't think less of yourself or settle for little. Set your mind on something good, and stop fearing.
verse.translation: Do not hold yourself in contempt, and do not keep it going on too little. Set your mind on what is truly good; don't be afraid. Pull yourself together.
verse.why: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

prasang.title: Vidula rouses her defeated son
prasang.summary: Kunti sends Yudhishthira the old story of Queen Vidula, who finds her son lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She shames, then reasons, then encourages him until he rises and fights for it again.
prasang.story_hook: A prince lay in bed after losing everything, until his mother walked in and refused to let him stay there.
prasang.lesson: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

verse.meaning: Vidula speaks to her son Sanjaya, who lies defeated after losing his kingdom. She tells him not to think less of himself or settle for a small life. She says to set his mind on what is truly good and stop being afraid. She pulls him together until he rises to fight for his own life again.
verse.for_you: Your parents are asking you to shrink into a smaller self that fits their story. Let Vidula's words hold you. Set your mind on what is truly good for you, not on their comfort. Stop fearing the fight.

verse.speaker: Ashtavakra
verse.setting: King Janaka asks the young sage Ashtavakra how a person becomes free.
verse.sanskrit: त्वया व्याप्तमिदं विश्वं त्वयि प्रोतं यथार्थतः । शुद्धबुद्धस्वरूपस्त्वं मा गमः क्षुद्रचित्तताम् ॥
verse.line: You are pure awareness, wider than any worry. Don't let your mind shrink into pettiness.
verse.translation: This whole universe is pervaded by you and strung on you. By nature you are pure awareness; do not fall into smallness of mind.
verse.why: You are more than your roles and worries; freedom starts with how you see yourself.

prasang.title: Janaka asks the boy-sage how to be free
prasang.summary: King Janaka, ruler of Mithila, asks the young sage Ashtavakra three questions: how to gain wisdom, freedom and dispassion. Ashtavakra answers at once: you are not the body or your roles but the awareness that watches them, and freedom is available now.
prasang.story_hook: A powerful king bowed before a boy whose body was bent in eight places, and asked him how to be free.
prasang.lesson: You are more than your roles and worries; freedom starts with how you see yourself.

verse.meaning: King Janaka asks the young sage Ashtavakra how to be free. Ashtavakra tells him that the whole universe is strung on him and that he is pure awareness. He warns Janaka not to fall into smallness of mind. The king is being asked to see himself as more than his roles and worries. The verse says freedom is available now, if he can stop shrinking.
verse.for_you: When your parents ask you to shrink to fit their story, they are asking you to fall into smallness of mind. You are not that smaller self. Hold onto the truth that you are wider than their worry, even when their words feel like they are closing in on you.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna on three kinds of food, effort, speech and giving.
verse.sanskrit: अनुद्वेगकरं वाक्यं सत्यं प्रियहितं च यत् । स्वाध्यायाभ्यसनं चैव वाङ्मयं तप उच्यते ॥
verse.line: Speak words that don't wound, that are true, kind and helpful. That is discipline of speech.
verse.translation: Speech that causes no distress, that is truthful, pleasant and beneficial, and the regular study of sacred texts: this is called austerity of speech.
verse.why: Speak kindly and truly, give without strings, and drop the show.
verse.misuse: Kind speech doesn't mean avoiding hard truths; it means saying them without cruelty.

prasang.title: Three kinds of food, offering, austerity and giving
prasang.summary: Food, offering, austerity and giving each come in three kinds. Speech should be true, kind and helpful; giving should expect nothing back; effort for show doesn't last.
prasang.lesson: Speak kindly and truly, give without strings, and drop the show.

verse.meaning: Krishna is explaining the discipline of speech. He says it should be true, pleasant and beneficial, and it should not cause distress. He is teaching Arjuna that how you speak is a form of austerity. The discipline is to drop the show and speak with care.
verse.for_you: When you speak to your parents today, let your words be true, kind and helpful. You do not have to wound them to be honest. Say what you need without cruelty. This is your discipline of speech.

verse.speaker: Brihaspati (retold by Bhishma)
verse.setting: Brihaspati counsels Indra on how to hold authority among difficult people.
verse.sanskrit: मृदुमप्यवमन्यन्ते तीक्ष्णादुद्विजते जनः / मातीक्ष्णो मा मृदुर्भूस्त्वं तीक्ष्णो भव मृदुर्भव
verse.line: People walk over the soft and fear the harsh. Be firm when it's needed, gentle when it's needed.
verse.translation: People look down even on the gentle, and they shrink from the harsh. Do not be only harsh, do not be only soft: be firm when firmness is needed and gentle when gentleness is.
verse.misuse: Firmness here means clarity, not cruelty.

matched.label: I need to set boundaries with family

verse.meaning: Brihaspati is speaking to Indra, who is struggling to lead people who push back. He tells him that if he is only gentle, the crowd will walk all over him. If he is only harsh, they will scatter. The truth is, you need both. Be soft with the soft, and be unmovable with the hard. This is not about being cruel. It is about knowing exactly where you stand and refusing to bend just because someone wants you to.
verse.for_you: When your parents push, you can be gentle about your care for them, but you can also be firm about your own life. You do not have to choose between them and your truth. You can hold both.

story.title: Parvati holds to her choice
story.story_hook: The sages came to talk Parvati out of it, and they listed every flaw in the man she had chosen.
story.summary: Reborn as Parvati, Sati resolves to marry Shiva and spends years in austerity. The seven sages come to test her, mocking Shiva as a homeless ascetic and offering her a better match. She answers that gold keeps its nature even in fire, and that the heart wants the one it has chosen.
story.lesson: Persistence is choosing the same thing again each day, even when others call it foolish.

anchor.speaker: Parvati
anchor.setting: Parvati answers the sages who mock her resolve to win Shiva through years of austerity.
anchor.sanskrit: सत्य कहेहु गिरिभव तनु एहा। हठ न छूट छूटै बरु देहा॥ कनकउ पुनि पषान तें होई। जारेहुँ सहजु न परिहर सोई ॥
anchor.line: Gold comes from stone, and even in fire it stays gold. Hold to what you are.
anchor.translation: You speak truly: this body was born of a mountain, so its resolve will not break, even if the body does. Gold too is born of stone, and even in fire it does not give up its nature.
anchor.why: Persistence is choosing the same thing again each day, even when others call it foolish.
anchor.misuse: Steadiness is not stubbornness; keep checking that the goal is still worth it.

prasang.title: Parvati holds to her choice
prasang.summary: Reborn as Parvati, Sati resolves to marry Shiva and spends years in austerity. The seven sages come to test her, mocking Shiva as a homeless ascetic and offering her a better match. She answers that gold keeps its nature even in fire, and that the heart wants the one it has chosen.
prasang.story_hook: The sages came to talk Parvati out of it, and they listed every flaw in the man she had chosen.
prasang.lesson: Persistence is choosing the same thing again each day, even when others call it foolish.

story.hook_title: The sages listed every flaw in the man Parvati had chosen
story.teaser: The sages listed every flaw in the man Parvati had chosen
story.for_you: Parvati held to her choice even when the sages told her she was wrong. Your love is real. The people who want you to shrink are not the ones who get to name what your life looks like. You do not have to choose between them and your truth. You get to choose both.

script: You are caught in two worlds right now. One world is the person you are becoming, the one you have built a real life with. The other world is the story your parents want you to live, a story where you shrink to fit their comfort. You feel like you lose a piece of yourself no matter what you choose.

Sita waits in the forest. She is alone, pregnant, and far from everything she knew. Ram has ordered Lakshman to leave her there, cut off from her husband, her home, and her name. She is innocent, but the gossip of the world has turned her into a question. She sends a message back to Ram. And Sita says:
अहं तु नानुशोचामि स्वशरीरं नरर्षभ. यथापवादः पौराणां तथैव रघुनन्दन.
In plain words: It isn't the hardship I mind most. It's what people are saying that wasn't true.

She says she does not grieve for her own hardship. What breaks her is the slander, the false talk that people are spreading about her time away. She is saying that injustice from those we love is a deeper wound than any forest or exile. The pain is not in her body. It is in the lie told about her by people who should know better. She is not asking to be defended. She is naming exactly what hurts her, and what does not.
Your parents are asking you to choose, but the gossip is not about you. It is about their comfort. A stranger's kindness can become home. Let that be your footing today.
The false talk is not your burden to carry.

depth.life: You sit with your phone and the weight of two years against their single question. You keep fighting because the smaller self they want you to become feels like a stranger. You are torn between the home you know and the life you have built, and both feel like they are asking you to disappear.
depth.points: The grief is not the choice itself, but the gossip that drives it. You are being asked to shrink so their story stays neat. A stranger's kindness, like Valmiki's, can become a home when the old one turns cold. The truth is in you, not in their comfort.
depth.practice: Write down one true thing about your relationship that your parents do not see, and read it once before you sleep.
depth.question: What part of yourself are you protecting right now?
